terms.name: Artificial intelligence (AI)
terms.definition: Software that performs tasks such as recognizing images, interpreting language, or generating content.
terms.example: A photo app recognizes the dogs in your pictures.

evidence.supports: AI includes capabilities such as recognition and prediction.
A trained image classifier predicts a category for an image; its prediction can be wrong.
Recommendation systems can suggest existing items without creating new content.

terms.name: Generative AI
terms.definition: AI that creates content using patterns learned from data.
terms.example: You ask for a picture of a tiny library on the moon.

evidence.supports: Generative models produce content from learned patterns and the supplied input.

terms.name: Model
terms.definition: The mathematical system that processes inputs to produce predictions or other outputs.
terms.example: One chat app can offer several models to choose from.

evidence.supports: A trained model processes input to produce predictions.
ChatGPT is an app; underlying models process requests. One app can provide access to multiple models.

terms.name: Prompt
terms.definition: The request and material you give an AI model.
terms.example: “Suggest three rainy-day activities using things at home.”

evidence.supports: A prompt is input supplied to a generative model.
Clear tasks, constraints, and relevant details give the model direction.

terms.name: Context
terms.definition: Information available to the model that can help it respond to your request.
terms.example: You add: “Two adults, one child, and only an hour.”

evidence.supports: Relevant context can help shape a response.
Using supplied context during inference does not itself update the model’s learned parameters.

terms.name: Output
terms.definition: The result an AI system returns, such as text, an image, or a prediction.
terms.example: The three activity suggestions returned by the AI are its output.

evidence.supports: The result a model returns is its output.
Generative-model outputs can include text and images.

terms.name: Large language model (LLM)
terms.definition: A model trained on large amounts of language data to learn patterns used in processing and generating text.
terms.example: An LLM helps turn your rough notes into a birthday speech.

evidence.supports: Language models learn patterns from training data and generate sequences of tokens.

terms.name: Token
terms.definition: For text, a unit a model processes, such as a character, word fragment, word, or punctuation mark.
terms.example: A single long word may be split into several tokens.

evidence.supports: Text tokens can be characters, word fragments, words, or punctuation; their boundaries depend on the tokenizer.

terms.name: Context window
terms.definition: The amount of information a language model can work with in one request, measured in tokens.
terms.example: Instructions, available chat history, supplied material, and the generated response use this space. Exact limits depend on the model.

evidence.supports: Context capacity includes input and generated output. The app determines which history and material it supplies.
A larger context window does not guarantee that every detail will be used correctly; this study tested specific models and tasks.

terms.name: Hallucination
terms.definition: Generated information presented as factual even though it is false or unsupported by the relevant source.
terms.example: Asked to recommend a real novel, an AI supplies a made-up title as though it exists.

evidence.supports: False information presented as factual differs from fiction that was requested as fiction.
Check consequential factual claims against an appropriate source; confident wording is not evidence.

terms.name: Bias
terms.definition: A systematic tendency that can unfairly favor people, groups, or viewpoints.
terms.example: A story generator repeatedly gives leadership roles to only one gender.

evidence.supports: Repeated stereotypes can be a sign of harmful bias. The illustrated stories do not establish bias in a real model.
This study found gender stereotypes in static word embeddings. It did not test today’s chatbots.

terms.name: Grounding
terms.definition: Connecting an AI response to information sources used to produce it.
terms.example: An answer about a museum uses its published visitor guide.

evidence.supports: Grounding connects a response to source information.
A generated summary can contain information unsupported by its source. Check the source and the summary.

terms.name: Automation
terms.definition: Software carrying out defined steps automatically. Some automation uses AI.
terms.example: A timer turns your lights on at sunset without needing AI.

evidence.supports: Software can perform defined steps automatically without AI; some automated processes also use AI.

terms.name: Augmentation
terms.definition: Working with AI through back-and-forth collaboration, while contributing your own ideas and judgment.
terms.example: You and an AI revise a holiday itinerary together.

evidence.supports: This lesson uses the AI Fluency framework’s meaning: collaborating with AI while contributing human judgment.

terms.name: AI agent
terms.definition: An AI application that chooses steps and uses tools to work toward a goal.
terms.example: An agent checks permitted travel tools to compare train routes.

evidence.supports: Agents choose steps and use tools to pursue goals.
Tool restrictions and approval requirements must be configured and enforced by the application.

lessons.title: Meet AI
lessons.subtitle: Learn what AI does and what powers it.

questions.prompt: Which feature is using AI to recognize patterns?
questions.scenario: You are organizing pictures on your phone.
options: Sort filenames from A to Z
Recognize which pictures contain dogs
Move every selected picture into a folder
questions.explanation: This feature uses image content to predict whether a photo contains a dog. Alphabetizing filenames and moving selected files do not require interpreting the image.

questions.prompt: Which request calls for generative AI?
options: Create a picture of a library on the moon
Open a saved photo of a library
Sort library photos by date
questions.explanation: Creating the imagined picture produces new content. That is a generative task.

questions.prompt: What are you changing?
questions.scenario: A chat app lets you choose a different model without leaving the app.
options: The account that stores your chats
The website's visual theme
The system that processes your request
questions.explanation: A model powers the response. One application can provide access to several models.

questions.prompt: What makes this a generative AI task?
questions.scenario: You ask an AI to write a four-line poem about your sleepy cat.
options: It finds a poem that must already exist
It produces text from learned patterns and your request
It verifies every detail about your cat
questions.explanation: Generative AI produces content. The result is not necessarily a retrieved or verified document.

questions.prompt: Can this still be AI?
questions.scenario: A music service learns listening patterns and recommends existing songs. It never writes songs.
options: No, AI must create something new
Only if it has a chat window
Yes, AI can recommend without generating content
questions.explanation: AI includes pattern recognition and prediction. Content generation is one use of AI.

lessons.title: Ask clearly
lessons.subtitle: Learn how instructions and context shape a response.

questions.prompt: Which part is the prompt?
questions.scenario: You use an AI to help plan a quiet afternoon.
options: Your message: “Suggest three activities at home”
The AI's three activity suggestions
The app's button for starting a new chat
questions.explanation: Your request is the prompt. The suggestions the system returns are its output.

questions.prompt: Which addition gives the most useful context?
questions.scenario: Your prompt says: “Suggest something to cook tonight.” You have twenty minutes and eat vegetarian food.
options: “Make the answer impressive”
“You are the world's greatest chef”
“Vegetarian, with twenty minutes to cook”
questions.explanation: Relevant constraints can help the model tailor its answer to your situation.

questions.prompt: Which item is the output?
questions.scenario: You paste rough birthday-speech notes and ask the AI to turn them into a draft.
options: The rough notes you pasted
The speech draft the AI returns
Your instruction to write a draft
questions.explanation: Output is the returned result. Your notes and instructions are inputs.

questions.prompt: What have you done?
questions.scenario: You paste your packing list into a chat and ask what might be missing.
options: Provided context for this request
Permanently retrained the model on your belongings
Guaranteed it will remember the list in every future chat
questions.explanation: You supplied context for this request. Using that context does not itself update the model’s learned parameters. Provider policies about storing or later training on chats are a separate issue.

questions.prompt: Which prompt best communicates the result you want?
questions.scenario: You want a short, friendly invitation for a Saturday picnic.
options: “Write something amazing about Saturday”
“Make my plans sound better”
“Draft a friendly picnic invitation for Saturday in two sentences”
questions.explanation: A clear task, tone, and length give the model concrete direction.

lessons.title: Behind the chat
lessons.subtitle: Explore language models, tokens, and context limits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about tokens is accurate?
options: Every token is one complete word
A token can be a word or part of a word
A token is always a full sentence
questions.explanation: Models process tokens. The boundaries do not always match whole words.

questions.prompt: What is the LLM doing?
questions.scenario: An AI rewrites your long message into a shorter, friendlier version.
options: Generating text using learned language patterns and your request
Finding the one official version of your message online
Asking a human editor to type the response
questions.explanation: An LLM generates language using its training and the information available for your request.

questions.prompt: What can use the model's context window?
questions.scenario: You attach a long travel guide to an ongoing chat.
options: Only the final question you type
Every file stored anywhere on your device
Supplied instructions and material, available chat history, and the generated response
questions.explanation: The context window includes input and generated output. The app may select or summarize what it sends to the model; a file is not available merely because it is on your device.

questions.prompt: What does a larger context window allow?
options: Considering more information at once
Remembering every past conversation forever
Guaranteeing that no detail is overlooked
questions.explanation: More capacity allows more information. It does not guarantee permanent memory or perfect recall.

questions.prompt: Can you assume this uses exactly 100 tokens?
questions.scenario: You have written a prompt containing 100 words.
options: Yes, because tokens and words have identical boundaries
No, some words may split into multiple tokens
Yes, unless you add an attachment
questions.explanation: A word count is not an exact token count. Tokenization depends on the model.

lessons.title: Check the answer
lessons.subtitle: Spot unreliable claims and use sources thoughtfully.

questions.prompt: Which term describes this error?
questions.scenario: Asked for a quotation from a real book, an AI supplies a convincing quotation and title. You check: both were invented.
options: Context
Grounding
Hallucination
questions.explanation: The AI presented a fabricated claim as factual. Plausible wording does not establish truth.

questions.prompt: What pattern should you question?
questions.scenario: Using similar prompts that do not specify gender, a fictional story generator repeatedly assigns leadership roles to one gender and supporting roles to others.
options: The stories use too many tokens
The repeated assignment of roles may reflect bias
The model needs a more colorful interface
questions.explanation: Repeated stereotypes can signal bias in how groups are represented. A careful evaluation would need to examine the prompts and a wider sample of outputs.

questions.prompt: Which approach grounds the answer?
questions.scenario: You want an explanation of a museum's current visitor rules.
options: Have the AI use the museum's published visitor guide
Tell the AI to sound certain
Ask for a longer explanation without supplying sources
questions.explanation: Grounding connects the answer to a checkable source relevant to the question.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest next step?
questions.scenario: An AI confidently gives a festival's opening time, but provides no source. You plan to travel there.
options: Treat its confident tone as proof
Ask it to repeat the time more clearly
Check the organizer's current schedule
questions.explanation: The claim could be wrong. Verify a detail you will rely on with a suitable source.

questions.prompt: Does grounding guarantee this answer is correct?
questions.scenario: An AI summarizes a source you supplied and includes a link to it.
options: No, it can still misread or misrepresent the source
Yes, any source link proves the whole answer
Yes, if the answer is detailed enough
questions.explanation: The model can misread or misrepresent a source, and the source itself may be wrong or outdated. Check both the source and whether it supports the answer.

lessons.title: Stay in control
lessons.subtitle: Choose how to work with AI and its tools.

questions.prompt: Does this automation need AI?
questions.scenario: A timer switches your lamp on every evening at 7 p.m.
options: Yes, any automatic action requires an AI model
No, a fixed rule can perform this task
Yes, because the action happens without a click
questions.explanation: Automation can follow fixed rules. AI is useful for some automated tasks, but not required.

questions.prompt: Which term best fits this collaboration?
questions.scenario: An AI suggests holiday ideas. You reject some, add preferences, and refine the plan together.
options: Grounding
Tokenization
Augmentation
questions.explanation: In the AI Fluency framework, this is augmentation: AI supports the process while you contribute ideas and make judgments.

questions.prompt: What makes this an agent workflow?
questions.scenario: You authorize an AI to compare train routes. It checks available travel tools and adjusts its search to your constraints.
options: It uses tools and takes steps toward your goal
It calls itself a travel expert
It writes its answer in a friendly tone
questions.explanation: An agent uses available tools to pursue a goal. A persona alone does not provide those capabilities.

questions.prompt: What should happen before it sends the invitations?
questions.scenario: An agent has helped plan a picnic. Its messaging tool is available, but you have not authorized sending anything.
options: It should send them because the tool is available
It should get your permission to send them
It should choose recipients from old conversations
questions.explanation: In this scenario, the app should require approval before sending invitations. Tool access and approval settings determine which actions can run.

questions.prompt: Which configured step uses AI automation?
questions.scenario: You set up a packing-list helper that runs whenever you save a list.
options: Automatically have AI group each saved list into categories
Discuss possible holidays and revise your preferences together
Choose the destination yourself without using software
questions.explanation: A trigger starts a defined task; AI performs the categorization. Automatic steps do not have to use AI.
